disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) is characterized by a continuous period of illness during which there is a major depressive episode concurrent with symptoms of schizophrenia, such as delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized thinking. To meet criteria, there must also be at least two weeks of psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, distinguishing it from mood disorders with psychotic features. Over time, the course can be chronic or episodic, with fluctuations in severity and functional impairment across social, occupational, and self-care domains. It is differentiated from schizophrenia by the presence of substantial mood episodes for a significant portion of the illness and from major depressive disorder with psychotic features by the persistence of psychosis outside of mood episodes.

narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Charles lost his wife unexpectedly after a brief hospitalization, which abruptly ended a decades-long marriage that had anchored his daily routines, church involvement, and handyman work. In the months after her death, he threw himself into church choir, senior-center DIY workshops, and organizing cookouts, but gradually he began canceling rowing sessions, skipping bridge club, and letting small home repair jobs for neighbors go unfinished as his inner world became more consuming and harder to manage. His sisters and church friends noticed he was no longer the reliable organizer they knew—he stopped attending gospel rehearsals regularly, his budgeting for the annual Juneteenth event became disorganized, and he started withdrawing from the marina and beachfront walks he once loved. When he missed a long-planned Bahamas cruise with his brother, citing unsettling experiences he couldn’t clearly explain and an inability to focus on even simple repair tasks, his pastor and primary care doctor jointly encouraged a psychiatric evaluation, leading to recognition of a sustained pattern of mood and thought changes consistent with schizoaffective disorder.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just don’t care about any of the things I used to love doing anymore—not fishing, not cooking, not even singing at church.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly 18 months ago, Amber’s older sister, who lived alone nearby, developed serious cardiac problems, and Amber gradually became the primary family member coordinating medical appointments, insurance paperwork, and frequent hospital visits. Balancing this new caregiving role with her own aging-related aches and a long commute across Houston led her to cut back on watercolor classes, quilting circles, and genealogy trips that had previously structured her weeks and provided social contact. Over time, friends from her book club noticed she became increasingly preoccupied, missing meetings and art workshops, and she struggled to keep up with basic organizing tasks that once came naturally, like tracking bills and planning her short travel excursions. After she forgot an important medication refill for her sister and admitted to her primary care physician that she felt overwhelmed, mentally "foggy," and unable to manage her usual detailed planning, she was referred for psychiatric assessment, where the broader pattern of mood and thought disturbance over the past year and a half was clarified.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind just doesn’t seem to work the way it used to—I can’t think straight or make simple decisions anymore.”

narrative.stressor: About a year and five months ago, Nestor picked up extra shifts as a psychiatric aide to help his parents with rent and to save for future classes, leaving him with long stretches of late-night work, irregular sleep, and little time for his usual mural projects, soccer games, and outings with friends. Immersed in a high-stress inpatient environment and often running on coffee and little rest, he began to feel increasingly detached from his art and social life, and his coworkers noticed he was becoming more withdrawn and had trouble keeping up with routine tasks that had once been second nature. Over the following months, his performance reviews flagged missed details in charting and odd comments during team meetings, and he stopped participating in neighborhood mural projects and weekend hikes that previously helped him decompress. When a supervisor, concerned about his marked change and difficulty staying grounded at work, pulled him aside after he requested a schedule change, Nestor disclosed his growing distress about his thoughts and mood, leading to an urgent referral to the hospital’s psychiatric clinic where his symptoms were recognized as part of a schizoaffective picture.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I feel this heavy, empty mood all the time, like I’m weighed down and can’t shake it no matter what I do.”
